title: Who has the best market forecast? You do
html:
People take photos beside the Charging Bull on Wall Street in New York City on Monday. Sticking out their necks, strategists at Goldman Sachs expect this bull market will persist through considerable headwinds.Spencer Platt/Getty Images

We are in the final six weeks of the year, which means that days are getting short, the holiday season is approaching and stock market forecasters are rolling out their predictions for next year.

Will 2027 deliver a boom, a bust or both? Relax, professional soothsayers have you covered.

Well, sort of.

Stock market forecasts tend to fall within a narrow range of outcomes that rarely stray far from the long-term average performance of about an 8-per-cent gain.

Risks and the possibility of outlier events, such as economic recessions, stock market crashes or double-digit rallies, may be discussed in these outlooks. But they won’t form the base case of any but the most attention-grabbing forecasts.

This steady-she-goes approach makes a lot of sense. Who wants to alarm investors with warnings of impending doom? And who wants to promise dazzling rallies when ho-hum performance is more likely?

In this context, strategists at Goldman Sachs are sticking out their necks this year.

They expect the S&P 500 will deliver a blistering total return – that is, with dividends – of 18 per cent through the end of 2027. That’s more than double the pace of an average return.

What’s even more remarkable is that the strategists expect this bull market will persist through considerable headwinds.

They expect corporate profit growth will slow to about 11 per cent next year, down from about 30 per cent this year, as spending on artificial intelligence moderates. The Fed will likely raise its key interest rate twice, in December and March.

A third headwind: This bull market is getting old.

“One striking contrast with past overextended bull markets is the lack of speculative mania in today’s market,” Ben Snider, chief U.S. equity strategist, said in a note.

Strategists at Morgan Stanley are also upbeat about next year.

They expect the S&P 500 will end the year at 8,700. That implies a gain of nearly 20 per cent from Monday’s close (or up 15 per cent from mid-November, when the outlook was made).

“The biggest change since our midyear outlook is how much more attractive risk has become,” Serena Tang, Morgan Stanley’s chief cross-asset strategist, said in a note.

“Stocks and corporate bonds have cheapened even as expectations for AI investment have risen. And of course, we’re heading into 2027 with more clarity on two big unknowns – the U.S. midterm elections are behind us and markets better understand the Federal Reserve’s reaction function.”

Will either prediction pan out exactly as outlined?

Probably not. There are a lot of moving parts here. As we saw last week, market downturns can spring out of nowhere, leaving market prognosticators scrambling for explanations.

Rallies can spring from unusual quarters, too. Which strategist saw Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as a reason to own stocks before Monday’s incredible rally?

Even when they fall short, market forecasts can be valuable tools, though. They can inform investors about some of the themes that are likely to develop in the coming year, preparing us for the ups and downs.

They can also challenge our biases toward either too much caution or too much optimism, giving us a reason to stay appropriately invested without fear or greed getting the best of us.

What the pros suggest is useful information to have tucked into your back pocket. But the best approach for most people is to maintain the right diversification, no matter what the outlook.

That means maintaining a consistent exposure to stocks and bonds, with perhaps some cash on the sidelines. That way, you’re prepared for when the pros are right – and when they’re wrong.

What’s your take for 2027? Let me know at dberman@globeandmail.com.

Investors found out on Monday, when Nvidia’s share price soared. Exchange-traded products designed to rise when Nvidia declines tanked 92 per cent.

An SNL commercial parody, called “Sister,” is getting a lot of attention – and for reasons that go well beyond the laughs. From AARP: “The sketch gets to the heart of what AARP research already shows to be true: There is a gender and workload imbalance in family caregiving.”

Chart of the day

Where you live in Canada will determine how long you’ll live. And if you want to live longer, you’ll not only need to move to a big city but to the right part of that city – the richer part. This chart from Mike Moffatt explains.

Today’s financial tool

Chatbots and spreadsheets can get you started on retirement planning. But made-in-Canada software from Optiml will give you a far more detailed plan and the ability to track your financial picture so you stay on track.

In the social sphere

Why read a 2027 outlook when you can watch it? Here, Jan Hatzius, chief economist at Goldman Sachs, and Dominic Wilson, senior adviser in the Global Markets Research Group, discuss the year ahead.

I had my reservations about watching the newly released “official music video starring Owen Cooper” to accompany The Beatles’ song, In My Life. My initial response: Actors? Give me John instead. But it was surprisingly touching.
